Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the appropriate initial radiologic assessment for shoulder instability.
List special radiographic views that are helpful for specific diagnoses.
Explain the use of magnetic resonance arthrography for increased sensitivity in patients with
shoulder instability.
Determine the appropriateness of CT and three-dimensional CT reconstruction.
Explain how to assess for on-track and off-track lesions.
Review normal MRI findings and variants.
Identify common shoulder instability pathology on magnetic resonance arthrograms.

Indications—Conventional radiographs are appropriate for patients experiencing shoulder
pain and have a history of trauma, dislocation, night pain, or chronic shoulder pain.1
Shoulder series—The standard shoulder series should include orthogonal views of the
shoulder, including a true AP view in the scapular plane, an AP view, an axillary view, and a
scapular Y view.
True AP view in the scapular plane
Visualizes the anterior greater tuberosity in profile
Beam of the x-ray is positioned perpendicular to the plane of the scapula
Arm is held in neutral rotation with the shoulder in slight abduction (dynamic loading of the
cuff and deltoid), which may reveal a decreased acromial humeral interval, indicative of
superior humeral head migration and rotator cuff disease
AP view
Visualizes the posterior aspect of the greater tuberosity and the lesser tuberosity in profile
Arm is held in internal rotation
Beam of the x-ray is positioned perpendicular to the coronal plane of the body
Axillary view
Necessary view in evaluation of glenohumeral joint instability
Shows the humeral head position in the glenoid fossa
Often overlooked but may detect occult, locked posterior shoulder dislocation in patients
who exhibit a lack of passive external rotation
Also helpful in evaluation of glenoid morphology in patients with glenohumeral
osteoarthritis and affords good visualization of the coracoid process, acromion, and distal
clavicle
Scapular Y view
Provides visualization of the coracoacromial arch
Reliable alternative for evaluation of glenohumeral subluxation and dislocation

Figure 1 AP (A) and axillary (B) radiographs of a shoulder demonstrate a posterior
dislocation. On the AP view, the humerus is held in internal rotation, and the proximal
humerus demonstrates the light bulb sign, which is characteristic of a posterior shoulder
dislocation. (Reproduced from Youm T, Takemoto R, Park BK: Acute management of shoulder
dislocations. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[12]:761-771.)
Computed Tomography
Indications
Glenoid bone loss: CT with three-dimensional reconstruction is the preferred advanced
imaging modality for determining the extent of glenoid bone loss in patients with shoulder
instability.1-4
Glenoid version: CT with three-dimensional reconstruction is the preferred imaging modality
for determining version and assessing glenoid bone stock. Three-dimensional reconstruction
images are more accurate than two-dimensional images in assessing glenoid version (Figure
2).
Assessing for risk of instability based on off-track and on-track combined glenoid and
humeral lesions

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The normal labroligamentous complex includes the glenohumeral ligaments (GHLs), the
labrum, and the long head of the biceps tendon (Figure 3; Resources 1 and 2).

Figure 3 Oblique sagittal MRI of a shoulder shows normal glenohumeral labroligamentous
structure (arrows). (Courtesy of Joshua A. Baumfeld, MD, FAAOS, Peabody, MA.)
The superior GHL originates on the supragenoid tubercle and inserts superior to the lesser
tuberosity. Its course parallels the coracoid process. It stabilizes the long head of the biceps
tendon (Figure 4).1-4
Figure 4 A and B, Axial MRIs of a shoulder (A and B) show a normal superior glenohumeral
ligament (arrows). (Courtesy of Joshua A. Baumfeld, MD, FAAOS, Peabody, MA.)
SEND FEEDBACK

Middle GHL: Originates on the anterior superior labrum or the glenoid neck and inserts on the
lesser tuberosity with the subscapularis tendon (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Coronal MRI of a shoulder shows the normal course of the middle glenohumeral
ligament (arrow). (Courtesy of Joshua A. Baumfeld, MD, FAAOS, Peabody, MA.)
Inferior GHL: Originates on the inferior glenoid labrum and inserts on the anatomic humeral
neck. It is the main static stabilizer of the shoulder with an anterior band, a posterior band,
and an axillary pouch (Figure 6).
Figure 6 MRIs of a shoulder show the glenohumeral ligament. A, Axial MRI shows the axillary
band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (arrow). B, Coronal MRI shows the inferior
glenohumeral ligament (arrow). (Courtesy of Joshua A. Baumfeld, MD, FAAOS, Peabody, MA.)
Anatomic variants are common, particularly of the middle GHL.

Labral morphology may be triangular, rounded, cleaved, flat, or absent (often from the 12-
o’clock to 3-o’clock positions).
Labral variants
Sublabral foramen (11% to 15%): A congenital detachment of the labrum in the 1-o’clock to 3-
o’clock position; noted by its smooth margination.
Sublabral recess: Synovial reflection at the 11-o’clock to 1-o’clock positions that parallels the
glenoid rim with smooth margination; should not be confused with a superior labrum anterior
to posterior (SLAP) tear.
Buford complex (2%): Absent segment of the labrum at 1-o’clock to 3-o’clock positions
associated with a thickened middle GHL.
Common shoulder instability findings on MRI (arthrogram):
Bankart lesion: Anterior capsulolabral pathology is best visualized on MRI with intra-
articular gadolinium. A detached and displaced labrum or simple undercutting of the
anteroinferior labrum with or without adjacent cartilage injury may be observed (Figure
7).1-4
Figure 7 Axial magnetic resonance arthrogram of a right shoulder shows a typical Bankart
lesion (arrow) with fluid extravasation between the labrum and the glenoid. (Reproduced
from Frank RM, Arciero RA, Erickson BJ, Trenhaile ST, Provencher MT, Verma NN: Shoulder
instability: An American perspective. Instr Course Lect 2018;67:415-432.)
Hill-Sachs lesion: A flattening of the posterolateral superior aspect of the humeral head
(impression fracture) (Figure 8)
SEND FEEDBACK

8/14

Figure 8 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction image of a humeral head shows a Hill-Sachs
lesion. Note the posterior indentation of the humeral head and the metaphysis.
(Reproduced from Streubel PN, Krych AJ, Simone JP, et al: Anterior glenohumeral instability:
A pathology-based surgical treatment strategy. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[5]:283-294.)
Bankart fracture: A fracture of the anterior/inferior glenoid, often associated with
disruption of the labroligamentous complex and periosteal elevation; larger fractures lead
to increased instability.
SLAP lesion: Magnetic resonance arthrography is the preferred imaging modality for
evaluation of SLAP lesions MRI without contrast is associated with poor sensitivity for SLAP
lesions. Clinical correlation and physical examination findings are essential to corroborate
MRI findings (Figure 9 and Figure 10); Resource 3).5,6
Figure 9 Illustration shows the Snyder classification of superior labrum anterior to
posterior tears. A, Type I: Local degeneration and fraying on the inner margin of the
superior labrum are noted. B, Type II: The superior labrum and the biceps tendon anchor

are detached from the superior glenoid rim. C, Type III: A bucket-handle tear of the superior
labrum is noted; the biceps anchor is intact. D, Type IV: The bucket-handle tear extends into
the biceps tendon. (Reproduced from Dreese JC, Casagrande D: Arthroscopic superior
labrum anterior-to-posterior repair, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic
Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 21-
30.)
Figure 10 A, An axial T2 magnetic resonance arthrogram image of the shoulder, where a
tear of the labrum can be seen on posterior aspect of the labrum consistent with a SLAP
tear. B, A T1 sagittal cut in which extravasation of the contrast can be seen above the
labrum, indicating a tear. (Reproduced from Morris BL, Vopat BG, Wong JE, Peebles LA,
Golijanin B, Provencher MT: Superior labrum and biceps pathology, in Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2022, pp 43-56.)
Spinoglenoid cyst: MRI is the preferred diagnostic imaging modality; ultrasonography of the
shoulder has not been shown to be effective in identifying spinoglenoid cysts.
Kim lesion: A concealed lesion of the posteroinferior labrum observed in patients with
posterior or multidirectional posteroinferior instability of the shoulder (Figure 11).

Figure 13 T2-weighted MRIs of a shoulder with a labral tear. A, Sagittal MRI (left) shows the
axis through which an oblique axial MRI (right) is obtained. B, Axial (left) and oblique axial
(right) MRIs show a posteroinferior labral tear. Note the serrated appearance (yellow circle)
of the posteroinferior labrum on the oblique axial image. (Reproduced from Sheean AJ,
Kibler WB, Conway J, Bradley JP: Posterior labral injury and glenohumeral instability in
overhead athletes: Current concepts for diagnosis and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg.
2020;2[15]:628-637.)
Humeral avulsion of the GHL: Avulsion of the inferior (anterior or posterior) GH, observed
in 5% to 10% of patients with glenohumeral instability; more common in males; may be
associated with a subscapularis tear (Figure 14).
Figure 14 Oblique coronal magnetic resonance arthrogram of a shoulder shows a humeral
avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (arrow). (Reproduced from Streubel PN, Krych AJ,
Simone JP, et al: Anterior glenohumeral instability: A pathology-based surgical treatment
strategy. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[5]:283-294.)
